blocks.text: In 2006, a Wharton scholar named Ravi Aron sat down with Shiv Nadar. Forbes had just valued Nadar at about ==$3 billion==, and HCL, the group he co-founded, had more than 36,000 employees. Aron asked how a Tamil man had ended up in the computer business in New Delhi. Nadar's answer began nowhere near a computer.
I come from rural stock. I studied in Tamil, never in English.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2006

blocks.text: He was born on ==14 July 1945== in Moolaipozhi, a village about 10 kilometres from the town of Tiruchendur, near the coast in what is now Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu. India was still a British colony. It became free when he was two.

Places like this did not usually produce computer tycoons. He was born into the Nadar community. In 2012 the Tamil business magazine Nanayam Vikatan described the community's usual trades as provisions, building materials, pulses and oil. That, it said, was exactly why a technology giant from this background surprised people.

photo.caption: The seashore at Tiruchendur. Moolaipozhi, where Shiv Nadar was born, lies about 10 kilometres from this town.
photo.author: Rahuljeswin

blocks.text: A father who kept moving

His father, Sivasubramaniya Nadar, was a judge. Forbes calls him a district judge, and Nanayam Vikatan calls him a district sessions judge. The job came with transfers, so the family did not stay put. Nadar describes a childhood spent "travelling from one place to another".

Forbes counted ==four schools== across the state by the time he finished. Each move meant a new classroom and new faces. He has never publicly said how that felt, so we will not guess. But notice what it demands of a child: again and again, you walk into a room where nobody knows you and you have to find your place.
His mother was Vamasundari Devi. He was the seventh of her eight children, and she sits at the centre of the best-known story he tells about money. You will meet that story in the next chapter.
Seventh of eight. Now picture that dinner table.

She also came from a remarkable family. Her brother was S.P. Adithanar, a barrister who was practising law in Singapore when Japan invaded. He came home to India and in November 1942 launched a Tamil daily from Madurai, Dina Thanthi, written so that ordinary Tamil readers could follow the news. It is still described as the largest-selling Tamil daily. So one of the boy's uncles had built a newspaper in his own language.

For example: in 1967, the year Shiv left college with an engineering degree, this same uncle was elected Speaker of the state assembly. A judge for a father and a newspaper founder and politician for an uncle: that is not the family of a boy with no one to look up to.

Here is a warning about how this life gets told. Some articles call his parents working-class and his roots humble. His own account is different. He says he had a "sheltered and protected upbringing", right up to one terrible moment in his teens. __The honest story is more useful than the rags-to-riches one: he did not start with nothing, but he did lose the ground under his feet.__
What was he like at five?

We looked hard for scenes from his earliest years, and we found almost none. In the interviews, articles and speeches we could read, there is no teacher's memory of the boy at five, no sibling telling stories, no favourite game. About his youth he says only that he "grew up like any adolescent boy at that age, oblivious to the harsh realities of life". He has kept this part of his life to himself.
No cute invented scenes here. If we can't source it, we don't print it.
The schools that remember him

What survive are the schools. One is Elango Corporation School in Madurai, a city-run school whose old building dates from 1937. Its headmaster, M. Rajendran, told the news agency ANI in 2019 that Nadar studied there in classes seven and eight. The Hindu dates his time there to 1952 to 1954. Another report puts him in "third form" in 1953.

Those dates do not add up, and you should know that. In 1952 he turned seven. A seven-year-old does not sit in class seven. Either the classes or the years are wrong. So treat his school timeline as rough, because no one has published the actual records. What everyone agrees on is that he sat in that building.

Another school is Town High School in Kumbakonam, which began on ==14 April 1864== as a primary school started by a retired head constable named Martin. The school names Nadar as an old student. Biographies online say he joined its first form, or class six, in June 1955 when he was nearly ten, and stayed until June 1957. The age fits, but we could not trace those dates back to a school record.

Now the detail we love. This is also the school of Srinivasa Ramanujan, one of the greatest mathematicians India has ever produced. He entered in January 1898 and left in 1904, and it was at this school that he found the maths book that set his mind on fire. His bronze bust now stands in front of the school library. So a judge's son from a village, who would one day build computers, did part of his growing up in the school that had shaped India's most famous mind with numbers.
Ramanujan's old school. Imagine hearing that name at ten.

photo.caption: Shiv Nadar at 64, at a British High Commission ceremony in Delhi, 2009. As a boy he studied only in Tamil.
photo.author: British High Commission, New Delhi

blocks.text: A childhood in Tamil

All of this schooling happened in Tamil. Forbes reports that he did not start speaking much English until he was ==22==. Today, thousands of Indian students sit in class feeling behind because their English is weak. Keep this fact in your pocket. The man who founded a group whose flagship, HCLTech, now has more than 2.2 lakh professionals in 60 countries did not speak much English as a teenager. __Your medium of instruction is a starting position. It does not decide how far you go.__

The family moves with his father's postings as a judge. He attends four schools in all.
Elango Corporation School, Madurai, by The Hindu's dates. Its headmaster says classes seven and eight, which does not fit those years.
Town High School, Kumbakonam, Ramanujan's old school. He would have been nearly ten.
St Joseph's in Trichy, where the story turns. That is the next chapter.

blocks.text: The schools got something back. In 2011 Nadar made what the principal called a sudden visit to the Elango school. People at the school later described cracked floors, seeping walls and toilets without water. A rebuild estimated at ==₹15 crore== followed, paid for by the old student, with smart classrooms and a library of 10,000 books. Town High School received computers and other equipment worth ₹80 lakh. He remembered exactly where he had started.

chapters.title: The Year the Floor Gave Way

blocks.text: By his teens, Shiv was at St Joseph's College Higher Secondary School in Trichy, a school in the Jesuit network that marked its 175th year in 2019. He went back to speak that year, aged 73. He remembered discipline as part of the school's culture, and support for people of different faiths. He remembered classmates who competed fiercely with him and did not sort one another by caste or religion. And he remembered doing very well.

photo.caption: St Joseph's College in Trichy. Shiv Nadar studied at its higher secondary school.
photo.author: அமுதவளன் ஞானாதிக்கம்

blocks.text: Forbes quotes his own verdict on himself in those years: "a very good student". Forbes India adds that he won scholarships through his student days. For a boy changing schools every few years, marks were the one thing that travelled with him. That is our reading, not his words, but look at what happened next.

At that 2019 speech he said something else that surprised people. He told the students that he had learned Hindi at St Joseph's for one year, picking up reading and writing, and that it had been of immense help. He spent most of his working life in north India and abroad. Hold on to this detail, because in the next chapter you will see him at the front of a very different kind of crowd.
A single year of school Hindi. It paid off for decades.
Grade 11

Then the event that split his life in two. When he was in ==grade 11==, his father died. By our arithmetic he was about 15 or 16, since he was at engineering college by 1962. He has not said how his father died or what the day was like, and that is his to keep. He has said what it did.
His early demise shook our entire family and especially me as till then I had a sheltered and protected upbringing.

The money trouble came fast. "The family started facing financial troubles and I was worried about my future," he wrote. The judge's position was gone, and a widow now had to bring up her children. He says his mother "had pretty much single-handedly brought us up".
He also noticed something about her during those years. It is a small thing, and it would come back decades later.
Despite being a single parent and dealing with all our hardships, I always saw her putting something away for religious reasons.

Jump ahead about 30 years. He is rich, and at dinner he is telling his mother how he plans to plough the money from a big deal back into the company. By his telling, she asks whether it is time to start giving back. The words struck him "like lightning", and a foundation followed in 1994, then a college named after the father he lost. __But the giving did not begin with the billionaire. It began with a widow who set money aside even when there was little to set aside.__
Watch the mother. She is the real first investor in this story.

For example: think about what a family loses when a judge's salary stops and the younger children are still in school. For a boy in that spot, the next stage of education depends on someone else's generosity or on his own marks. Shiv needed both. Forbes India says he won scholarships all through his student days, and he says his college degree came on a full one.
What he did not do

Founder stories love a teenage hustle: the stall, the resale racket, the radio built in a bedroom. We searched for Shiv Nadar's. We found no first deal, no side business and no gadget in any report, interview or article of his that we could read. We also found nothing reliable about bullying, his favourite books or his school friends. If he had such a story, this is a man who has had many chances to tell it.

As far as the record shows, the teenage Shiv Nadar studied, did well and worried about money. __You do not need a childhood startup to build a giant company at 31.__ If you are 17 and your only "venture" so far is your marks, you are in good company. His first company came 13 years after this stage of life, once he knew an industry from the inside.
No hustle at 16. A company at 30. Breathe.
A Tamil boy in a Tamil storm

Outside the classroom, the air was changing. His uncle Adithanar founded a party called We Tamils in 1958 and pressed for a Tamil nation. In 1960, by the account of Australia's public broadcaster SBS, he organised protests at which maps of India without Tamil Nadu were burned. We do not know how close the teenager was to this uncle or what he thought of those protests. Nothing we found says.

Then there was the matter of language. Under the Constitution's timetable, English was to stop being India's associate official language on ==26 January 1965==, leaving Hindi on top. Across the Tamil-speaking south that date felt like a threat, and by 1963 the DMK party was calling for direct action. A Tamil-medium boy growing up in those years could hardly have missed it. He would be 19 when the date arrived, and it would nearly get him shot.
Madurai again, and one scholarship

After school he went back to Madurai for a pre-university course at the American College, the step between school and an engineering degree. This old missionary college became a collegiate department in 1881 and moved to its present campus in 1906. Its proud alumni list today runs from Shiv Nadar to G. Venkataswamy, the founder of Aravind Eye Hospitals.

photo.caption: The Main Hall of The American College, Madurai, where Shiv Nadar did his pre-university course.
photo.author: எஸ்ஸார்

blocks.text: Then the door opened. He won a place at PSG College of Technology in Coimbatore to study engineering, and with it a full scholarship. In the same 2018 article he says he was 21 when this happened. His other dates point to about 17: he was a third-year student in January 1965, and his class graduated in 1967 after five years. Whatever the age, he has no doubt about what it meant.

That was truly the beginning of my story and the genesis of HCL as none of it would have been possible if my college education wasn't sponsored through a scholarship offered by the philanthropists who started PSG Tech.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, on his PSG scholarship, Dataquest, 2018

blocks.text: Read that again. He does not say the story began with the microprocessor, or with the day he quit his job. He says it began with strangers paying for a grieving teenager's education. Much of what he later did with his money grows out of this one fact. He says he only connected those dots decades later, at that dinner table with his mother.

blocks.title: Being sheltered ends. Plan for it.
blocks.text: Shiv Nadar's safe childhood ended without warning at about 16. What he credits for getting him through is education and scholarship, and those rested on the record he had already built in the one currency a teenager controls: marks. If your family is comfortable now, build yours anyway.

chapters.title: Six Men and a Rooftop Room

blocks.text: To see why his college mattered so much, you need one old family story. In 1926 the four sons of P.S. Govindasamy Naidu of Coimbatore divided their inheritance. They split it into ==five== equal shares, not four. The fifth went to charity, and they called it "The Fifth Brother". That brother went on to found PSG College of Technology in 1951, the place that later paid for Shiv Nadar's degree.
Four brothers gave charity an equal share. It paid for Shiv's degree.

photo.caption: The arch of PSG College of Technology, Coimbatore. Shiv Nadar spent five years here.
photo.author: Tm.dinesh

blocks.text: Grim food and a 4 a.m. alarm
He spent five years at PSG, and at his class's golden jubilee in December 2016 he told the old boys what he remembered. First, the food.
We were allotted the old hostel, and the food was comparatively grim there.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, PSG Tech class of 1967 reunion, 2016

blocks.text: He drew a surprising lesson from it. It taught him that life was going to be like this, he said, and it gave him "the strength to go on and establish a company in a land that is alien to me". His roommates were R. Srinivasan, who later founded Redington and went on to chair the college Shiv built, and P. Shanmugavelu. They had a problem with Shiv. He woke at 4 a.m.
When you wake up early you disturb others (laughs). So, I would run for 5000m every morning.

He was still speed-walking 3,000 metres at 71. On Saturdays there was idli, sambar and chutney for breakfast, and he says they ate it with love. He also told a Chennai audience that he sometimes got so bored in class that he would ask the professor for permission to go to the library and read something else. Forbes quotes the frustration behind that habit.
I was never allowed to do anything cross-disciplinary. Why can't an engineering student learn physics?

For example: how does a boy taught only in Tamil learn English? Partly at the movies. "In PSG, they used to teach English in Tamil," he told his classmates, to laughter. On Fridays the college screened English films, and on Sundays the friends went into town for more. By his own count he saw "some 1,000 movies" in college. That is about four a week for five years, so allow for a happy memory. But this is how he remembers learning the language he would later do business in.

Two teachers shaped him, he said: R. Subbayyan and G.R. Damodaran, the college's founding principal, known to everyone as GRD. "Professor Subbayyan, contradictory to his nature, was very patient with me, and so was GRD," he recalled.

Another student, who joined in 1955, left a picture of the kind of man GRD was. That boy could not pay his ₹450 admission fee and stood at the gate in tears. GRD got out of his car, signed "Yes. Admit" in green ink on the bonnet, and later handed over ₹300 of his own money for clothes and shoes. That was the place that took in a widow's son.
The day he nearly faced bullets

In January 1965 Shiv was 19 and in his third year. Hindi's date with destiny had arrived. On 25 January, he later told a PSG audience, police baton-charged students near a post office in Coimbatore. The next day came a rumour that two students of Madurai Medical College had been shot. About ==5,000 students== from colleges across the city marched to the Collector's office to demand answers. In his words, they marched "with me in front".

The officials told them that there were shoot-at-sight orders against anyone turning violent. He has never forgotten how that felt. As the crowd began to break up, somebody called out that since they had come this far, they should torch two or three buses. The boy at the front had to answer, with a crowd behind him and shoot-at-sight orders hanging over them all.
Someone was holding a gun and calling your bluff. It was as big a risk you can possibly take.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, recalling 1965, at PSG College of Technology, 2012

blocks.text: "But I politely turned down this dangerous appeal," he said. This is his version, told 47 years later, and we did not find an independent record of his part in it. But it is the first time in the record that we see the adult Shiv Nadar: __willing to take a huge risk, and clear about which risks are stupid.__ He summed up those years this way: they taught "courage, resilience, leadership and optimism".
Led an anti-Hindi march at 19. Told students to learn Hindi at 73.

The irony was not lost on his friends. At a talk in Chennai, a fellow PSG graduate teased him about leading those campus protests and then becoming a king in the Hindi heartland. Nadar chuckled that marrying Kiran had not helped his image either.
The job he usually skips

He graduated in 1967 with a degree in electrical and electronics engineering. Dataquest says he topped his class. His first job was at Cooper Engineering, a Walchand group company in Pune, and the Tamil magazine Nanayam Vikatan says he stayed about a year. That is nearly all anyone has written about it. When a reader asked him in 2011 why he started HCL, he simply began: "I started my career with DCM in 1968." Cooper did not even get a mention.
I first saw a city when I was 22.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2006

blocks.text: Here is a neat fit. He turned 22 in July 1967, which is the year he went to Pune. Madurai and Trichy are hardly small towns, so we read his line as a feeling more than a fact. __Your first job does not have to be a chapter of your legend. It can be a one-year stop on the way out of your village.__
Delhi, and the people who changed everything

In 1968 he reached Delhi and DCM, short for Delhi Cloth & General Mills, one of India's top five private groups. It made textiles, food, chemicals, fertilisers and more, and Business Standard later called it "a nursery for talent like Shiv Nadar". He began in the textile division, as part of what his foundation calls "the elite DCM management trainee system". How elite? His future partner Arjun Malhotra, who joined as a senior management trainee around 1970, remembered about ==30,000 applicants== for 8 to 12 places.

Malhotra was a good story in himself. He was an IIT Kharagpur graduate headed for a PhD in America and a career at NASA, and he took the DCM job mainly because the father of the girl he loved insisted on a confirmed job first. He deferred his Stanford place for one year, then for five. He never went. "The first person I met was Arjun," Nadar recalled. The others in that circle all worked at DCM too, and they were all about the same age.
We used to hang out together, crib together, have fun together, work together.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to CNBC-TV18, on his DCM friends

blocks.text: Your future co-founders are the people you crib with at work. Look around.

Above them stood Vinay Bharat Ram, the family's young executive, who had once been ordered by his own father to stamp in at the workers' gate before 6:30 every morning, despite his American MBA. Nadar names him as a role model who "mentored me in DCM". Delhi gave him one more person. Kiran worked at the advertising agency MCM, and Shiv was a client. "I went to work in Delhi at 23, and fell in love with my wife," he told Wharton, a Punjabi who was as far from his Tamil world as language could make her. Dataquest says that she, along with Arjun, egged him on to go out on his own.
The calculator years

In 1971 DCM decided to enter electronics, and Vinay Bharat Ram picked Nadar, then about 26, to run sales and marketing in a new unit, DCM Data Products. Malhotra worked alongside him. Their rival was the old Facit mechanical calculator, where you turned a lever by hand to add up numbers. They wanted to sell a desktop electronic one, made in India, with imported chips.

photo.caption: A Swedish Facit mechanical calculator built in 1954. Machines of this make were the competition DCM's electronic calculators had to beat in India.
photo.author: Hannes Grobe

blocks.text: For example: launching was not simple. Malhotra remembers American chip suppliers failing one after another. The team went from a Varadyne chip set to a Mostek one before settling on Electronic Arrays, and he says that delayed the launch. The calculator finally came out in 1972.

It worked brilliantly. By Malhotra's account, DCM held about ==80 percent== of the market. In 1974 Nadar sold some 300 units of a programmable model, the 1080 PS, and became known inside DCM as a sales wizard. Dataquest says he was among the highest-paid executives in Delhi in the early 1970s. He was under 30, with a good salary at a top company, and he was frustrated.
Though I was a success in all parameters at the time - a high-paying job, enough responsibilities, a highly successful venture, but still the restrictions were frustrating.

The restrictions had a name: the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act. It made life hard for big private groups entering new businesses. The team had gone beyond calculators and designed real computers, including a 16-bit machine, and the first microprocessors were just arriving. They went to the management and said let us sell this. DCM's lawyers warned that it could upset the government and put the group's other businesses at risk. The answer, in effect, was no.
A few of my colleagues and I could see that this was it. If we quit now and get started, there is a realistic chance of us making it.

He did not jump blindly. Dataquest and the writer Dinesh Sharma both describe him reading Electronics Commission reports and consulting its people. He narrowed his choice to two fields, medical electronics and computers, then picked computers. __That is the part founder stories skip: the walkout looked dramatic, but the choice was researched.__
One envelope

The moment came in ==October 1975==, by Sharma's account, at a DCM Data Products conference for sales and marketing staff. Nadar talked to colleagues informally and persuaded ten of them to leave. The next day they resigned together. Ten resignations went in one single envelope, and Dataquest calls the parting "acrimonious". Six stayed the course: Shiv Nadar, Arjun Malhotra, Ajai Chowdhry, Subhash Arora, Yogesh Vaidya and D.S. Puri.
Ten resignations. One envelope. Imagine being the person who opened it.

Then Malhotra's relatives weighed in. Leave a big company and a secure job? They thought he had gone crazy. When he told people microprocessors would change the world, he says, they assumed he "must be high on pot or something". "It was complete bravado," he later said of the whole plan. Years afterwards, his Wharton interviewer asked Nadar whether he had bet the family ranch.
What family ranch? I had barely worked for seven or eight years and had become a marketing manager.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2006

blocks.text: Nobody had a rich father to fall back on. "No one came from a business family; everyone came from a service family," Malhotra said. There was no venture capital, and banks wanted collateral. So they scraped. "We borrowed, pooled our savings and, in one case, even sold a car," Chowdhry wrote 50 years later. Dataquest once reported that Nadar borrowed from his provident fund. They had a target too, and it was funny for a computer company: DCM's fertiliser plant turned over ₹100 crore, so they told each other they would build their own "fertilizer plant".

items.label: the six founders' pooled capital, by most accounts
spent at once on a Bombay office, as Malhotra recalls it
what was left to actually run the business
free credit on calculators that kept them alive

blocks.text: The rooftop

They called the company Microcomp. The name was taken straight from DCM: it was DCM's name for a machine the team had worked on, and DCM had not bothered to register it. The company began in Nadar's own home in South Delhi and moved quickly to a barsati, a small room on the roof of a bungalow in Golf Links, owned by Malhotra's grandmother. She gave it free. It also put one of Delhi's poshest addresses on their business cards, so people might think these young men had old money behind them.

Soon they spread down into her house. Each morning they rolled up the bedding and turned the bedrooms into offices, and each evening they gave the rooms back. "And she became our receptionist," Malhotra says, chatting with waiting visitors. __One of India's biggest technology groups began on free rent, a borrowed name and somebody's grandmother.__
Very important for first-time founders: an address is marketing. A free one is better.

For example: the money nearly vanished on day one. Bombay was the big market, and rent-control rules meant you effectively had to buy an office. As Malhotra recalls it, ₹1.25 lakh of their ₹1.75 lakh went on 953 square feet in Bombay. That left ==₹50,000== to run a six-man national business. Then they spread out in pairs: two in Calcutta, two in Bombay, two in Delhi. Why pairs? "You need two people, one to cheer the other one up and say it's okay."
They also made rookie mistakes, and one of them is funny now. They knew calculators. They did not yet know how a business pays its taxes.

After we had done our calculations pertaining to costs, selling prices and margins, we realised that we had to pay something called the excise duty. Since it was too late, we decided to cut our margins rather than re-do the maths.

Their luck came from their old reputation. They had meant to make calculators themselves, but Ved Luthra of the TV maker Televista came to them. He could make calculators but could not sell them. The deal: sell mine, split the profit, and pay me after ==90 days==. Malhotra explains the trick: with 90 days to pay and customers paying in about 30, they held someone else's cash for about two months. Televista soon became India's top-selling calculator brand, and the cash went into developing a computer.
That was the time when I truly understood what cash flow is, and what profit is, and what reserves mean.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2006

blocks.text: Within about six months the business was humming. Nadar and Malhotra pulled back from selling and began working on a real computer, while the others kept the calculator cash flowing. __This is the cleverest move in the whole story: they did not raise money for their dream. They ran a boring business that paid for it.__

photo.caption: A Rockwell PPS-4 chip. Malhotra says the founders' first machines were based on this four-bit microprocessor.
photo.author: Christian Bassow

blocks.text: The licence

Then the wall. They had naively assumed they could simply build computers. But only government companies, central or state, were allowed licences to make them. Their answer was to find a state body that had one. The Uttar Pradesh Electronics Corporation, UPTRON, held a licence that covered computers but was making only TVs, and it agreed to a joint company. "They had the licence. We had the technology," Chowdhry wrote.

Look at how the deal was built. Total equity was just ==₹20 lakh==. UPTRON took 26 percent and the founders 25 percent. The other 49 percent was supposed to be sold to the public, but going public would have cost more than the ₹9.8 lakh it would raise. So the founders' calculator company, Microcomp, held that block, and the young men ended up with 74 percent.
A state partner with 26 percent. The founders kept control.
Being partnered with a state body also gave them the right to a grand name: Hindustan Computers Limited. Chowdhry said it was big, Indian and patriotic. It was, he said, perfect.
Interestingly, our toughest challenge was not designing or making computers but getting the government's approval to produce them.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2006

items.text: Joins DCM in Delhi as a management trainee, in textiles.
Picked to run sales and marketing at the new DCM Data Products.
Ten executives resign in one envelope. Six form Microcomp with about ₹1.87 lakh.
Hindustan Computers Limited is set up with UPTRON.

blocks.text: So in ==August 1976==, a few weeks after his 31st birthday, the judge's seventh child co-founded a computer company in a new industrial township called Noida. "I was 31, and I was the oldest," he remembered. He had no table of his own. The company did not yet have a computer to sell. As Chowdhry wrote half a century later, what it had was "a brochure for a computer that did not yet exist". What happened to that brochure is the next part of the story.

blocks.title: Fund the dream with something boring
blocks.text: The founders wanted to build computers, but they could not afford to. So they sold someone else's calculators on 90-day credit until the cash paid for the real work. Before you raise money for your big idea, ask what simple business in your own field could pay for it.

factCheck.method: Built first from Shiv Nadar's own words: his signed articles in Dataquest (2018) and Mint (2015), his Knowledge at Wharton interview (2006), his CIOL reader answers (2011), and press reports of his speeches at PSG Tech (2012, 2016) and St Joseph's, Trichy (2019), plus a Chennai International Centre report, published in 2023, of a talk (the event itself appears to be older). The founding story comes from co-founder Arjun Malhotra's Computer History Museum oral history (2018) and Mint interview (2009), Ajai Chowdhry's 2026 anniversary post as reported by Business Today and CNBC-TV18, the Dataquest profiles of 2002, 2007 and 2010, and Dinesh Sharma's book The Outsourcer. Sharma's p. 111 was read through an online page view, and the citation points to the publisher's page. Commons photo authors and licences were taken from the Commons API. A retail-finance biography (CapitalVia), Wikipedia and quote sites were used as leads only, except that Wikipedia is cited once to report that the 1955 to 1957 school dates are in circulation. Ages and the estimate for his father's death are our own arithmetic from his birth date and are labelled as such. Almost nothing reliable is public about his life before about 13, and the book says so.

disputed.claim: When he attended Elango Corporation School, Madurai
disputed.note: The Hindu says 1952 to 1954, a Times of India report summarised by Swarajya says third form in 1953, and headmaster M. Rajendran told ANI classes seven and eight. He turned seven in 1952, so these do not fit together. A later date, such as the late 1950s, would suit the classes, but no source says so. The book states the conflict.

disputed.claim: Town High School, Kumbakonam, June 1955 to June 1957
disputed.note: The school confirms he is an old student. The exact dates appear on Wikipedia and on copycat blogs without a checkable record, and they also clash with The Hindu's Madurai dates. Reported in the book as unverified.

disputed.claim: His age on joining PSG Tech
disputed.note: His 2018 Dataquest article says 21. A PTI report of his 2012 speech has him as a third-year student in January 1965, and the 2016 TOI report has five years ending with the class of 1967. That points to joining at about 17, around 1962. We use about 17 and flag it.
14 July 1945 is the date in Business Today and the PSG profile's info box. The body of the same PSG profile says 1946. We use 1945.

disputed.claim: 'I first saw a city when I was 22'
disputed.note: His own words to Wharton, also repeated by Dataquest. But he had already studied in Madurai, Trichy and Coimbatore. We quote him and say we read it as a feeling more than a fact. Its fit with his 1967 move to Pune is our inference.

disputed.claim: 'I got my PhD in engineering in Coimbatore'
disputed.note: The Wharton transcript has him saying PhD, and Vikatan also mentions a doctorate. The PSG, Forbes and Times Now accounts all describe an engineering degree, and his honorary doctorate came from Madras University in 2007. We say degree.

Times Now says working-class parents, and a family-tree website calls his father a state government clerk and the family Tamil Brahmin. Nadar himself, Forbes and Vikatan say judge, and his own account is 'sheltered and protected'. We follow his account and reject the website.

disputed.claim: What his mother said about giving back
disputed.note: Three versions exist: 'Don't you think it is time to start giving back?' (Dataquest 2018), 'Why don't you give some of this back to society, maybe build something more than just HCL?' (Mint 2015), and the CIC report's account that she said his money had helped no one beyond his family. The book paraphrases.

Rs 1.87 lakh in Dataquest 2010, Sharma and Chowdhry 2026. Rs 1.75 lakh in Malhotra's oral history, Business Today 2008 and Dataquest 2007. Rs 1.83 lakh in a Dataquest 2002 timeline. About Rs 1.8 lakh in Chowdhry's 2012 Mint interview. About $16,000 in Nadar's Wharton interview. Rs 18,700 in Business Today 2023 and others looks like a misprint. We use Rs 1.87 lakh, and Rs 1.75 lakh only when telling Malhotra's Bombay office arithmetic.

Six by Malhotra, Chowdhry and Dataquest 2010. Chowdhry said in 2002 that two more joined at HCL's founding, making eight, and Sharma says S. Raman joined months later. Nadar himself wrote 'seven of my colleagues'. We say six left to form Microcomp and do not state a final count for HCL.

disputed.claim: When and how they decided to leave
disputed.note: Sharma says an October 1975 sales conference, with resignations the next day. Dataquest 2002 says 1975 over coffee and snacks. Rediff 2007 says a canteen lunch in 1976, with an exit in the summer of 1976. Chowdhry's 2026 post says 1976. Malhotra says 1975. We use Sharma's account because it is the most specific and fits Malhotra and Dataquest.

disputed.claim: Who ran what at DCM Data Products, and Nadar's age in 1971
disputed.note: Dataquest 2010 says Nadar headed sales and marketing, with Malhotra as deputy, and that he was 23 in 1971. Malhotra's oral history says he himself was given field operations. Nadar says he headed the unit from 1971. Born in 1945, he was 25 or 26 in 1971, not 23. Dataquest also calls Malhotra an IIT Kanpur man, but he says Kharagpur. We use 'about 26' and Kharagpur.

Dataquest 2010 says DCM launched its 1101 computer in 1975. Malhotra says the group's lawyers blocked the computer plan, and that DCM chose to go to market only after the team left. We describe the legal block as Malhotra tells it and do not state whether the launch came before the walkout.

disputed.claim: Calculator launch month and DCM's market share
disputed.note: Malhotra says early 1972, Dataquest says August 1972. We say 1972. The 80 percent share is Malhotra's memory and has not been independently confirmed.

disputed.claim: Why DCM's calculator launch was delayed
disputed.note: Malhotra recalls that the chip suppliers, including Mostek, were failing at the time. As far as we know Mostek itself carried on for years after this, so the book says only that he remembers suppliers failing and that the team changed chip sets.
The account of leading 5,000 students and refusing to burn buses comes only from Nadar's own 2012 speech as reported by PTI. We found no independent record of his role, and the book says so.
